t: Phoenician was spoken in the cities of the northern Levant and carried by Tyro-Sidonian trade and colonies across the Mediterranean, where it became a lingua franca of the maritime world in the Iron Age.

Its alphabet, an abjad that wrote only consonants, passed to the Greeks and, through the Etruscans, to the Romans, and is generally believed to be at least a partial ancestor of almost all modern alphabets.

Almost nothing written on papyrus or parchment survived the damp coasts, so the language is known from about 10,000 inscriptions; a bilingual found in Malta let Jean-Jacques Barthélemy decipher it in 1758.
dyk: The word gorilla comes from Punic: Hanno the Navigator’s interpreters gave the name to a tribe of hostile ‘hairy people’ in the Gulf of Guinea, it passed into Greek as gorillai, and in 1847 Thomas S. Savage applied it to the western gorilla.
ev: The alphabet, first attested on inscribed bronze arrowheads, comes to be called Phoenician rather than Proto-Canaanite
Phoenician loses its old case endings, as Akkadian spellings of the name ‘Gift of Baal’ show
The Pyrgi Tablets are inscribed in Etruscan and Phoenician
Punic writers begin to mark final vowels with the letter aleph
Carthage is destroyed, after which the cursive Neo-Punic script becomes predominant
Phoenician seems to die out in the eastern Mediterranean
Punic, the western form of the language, seems to die out, perhaps lingering into the 9th century
Jean-Jacques Barthélemy deciphers the alphabet from the Cippi of Melqart, a Greek and Punic bilingual

f.family: Semitic; Northwest Semitic, Canaanite subgroup; similar to and mutually intelligible with Biblical Hebrew; dialects described as Tyro-Sidonian (the source of Punic) and Byblian
f.script: the Phoenician alphabet, an abjad of consonants only, called Proto-Canaanite until the mid-11th century BCE and Phoenician after 1050 BCE; the more cursive Punic and Neo-Punic forms; Punic also written in Greek letters (1st century BCE) and Latin letters (3rd and 4th centuries CE)
f.earliest: inscribed bronze arrowheads of the mid-11th century BCE; about 10,000 Phoenician and Punic inscriptions in all, among them the Ahiram sarcophagus, the Kilamuwa Stela, the Karatepe bilingual, the Nora Stone and the Pyrgi Tablets
f.status: extinct; in the east it seems to have died out in the 1st century BCE, while its western form, Punic, survived until the 6th century CE, perhaps even into the 9th
